title: Kinematics
lede: The math of motion: four equations that predict where anything will be and how fast it's going. Then the most practical use of physics a driver will ever need: stopping distance.

sections.md:
## The quantities
| Symbol | Quantity | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Δx | displacement (change in position, with direction) | m |
| v₀ | initial velocity | m/s |
| v | final velocity | m/s |
| a | acceleration (rate of change of velocity) | m/s² |
| t | time | s |

**Velocity has direction**; speed doesn't. Pick a positive direction at the start of every problem and stick to it. Slowing down while moving forward means **negative** acceleration.

## The four equations (constant acceleration)
1. **v = v₀ + at** (no Δx)
2. **Δx = v₀t + ½at²** (no v)
3. **v² = v₀² + 2aΔx** (no t)
4. **Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t** (no a)

**How to choose:** list the three quantities you know and the one you want. Pick the equation that contains exactly those four. Each equation is missing one variable; choose the one missing the variable you don't know and don't need.

sections.title: Merging onto the highway
sections.problem: A truck accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s at 0.75 m/s². How long does it take, and how far does it travel?
steps: Known: v₀ = 10, v = 25, a = 0.75. Want: t, Δx.
Distance: Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t = ½(35)(20) = 350 m.
sections.answer: **20 seconds and 350 m**, longer than most on-ramps. That's why heavy trucks build speed earlier and need room to merge.

sections.md:
## Free fall
Near Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, everything falls with the same acceleration: **g = 9.8 m/s² downward**, whatever its mass. Galileo argued this; astronaut David Scott demonstrated it on the Moon in 1971 by dropping a hammer and a feather, which landed together in the airless conditions.

If you drop something from rest, with down as positive: **v = gt** and **d = ½gt²**.
- After 1 s: falling 9.8 m/s, fallen 4.9 m.
- After 2 s: 19.6 m/s, fallen 19.6 m.
- After 3 s: 29.4 m/s, fallen 44.1 m.

sections.q: Ignoring air resistance, a bowling ball and a tennis ball dropped together…
sections.why: Same acceleration, g, regardless of mass.

sections.md:
## Projectiles: two independent motions
A thrown or launched object moves **horizontally at constant velocity** (no horizontal force, ignoring air) while **falling vertically** with acceleration g. The two motions don't affect each other.

Surprising result: a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height at the same instant hit the ground at the **same time** (on flat ground, ignoring air resistance). The fired one just lands much farther away.

## Stopping distance: physics on the road
**Total stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance**

- **Reaction distance** = speed × reaction time. You keep moving at full speed while you notice and react.
- **Braking distance** = v² ÷ (2a), from equation 3 with v = 0.

The **v²** is the important part: **double your speed, and braking distance quadruples**. Heavy loaded trucks also typically decelerate less sharply than cars, and air brakes add a short delay before they fully engage.

sections.title: Run the numbers
sections.problem: A loaded truck travels at 29 m/s (about 65 mph). Assume a 1.5 s reaction time and braking deceleration of 4.5 m/s². What's the total stopping distance?
sections.answer: **About 137 m (≈ 450 ft)**, roughly one and a half football fields, under these assumed conditions. On a wet road, with worn brakes or a heavier load, it's longer. Following distance isn't politeness; it's this math. (Your CDL manual gives the official guidance.)

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Velocity and acceleration can point opposite ways** (braking).
- **At the top of a throw, velocity is 0 but acceleration is still g.** It never switches off.
- **Units:** convert mph to m/s (1 mph ≈ 0.447 m/s) before using the equations.
- **Constant acceleration only.** These equations don't apply if acceleration changes.

practice.q: A car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s. Acceleration?
Starting at 5 m/s with a = 2 m/s², what's the velocity after 6 s?
Dropped from rest, how far does an object fall in 2 s? (g = 9.8)
Dropped from rest, speed after 3 s? (g = 9.8)
At the very top of a ball's upward flight, its acceleration is…
Reaction distance at 25 m/s with a 2 s reaction time?
A horizontally fired bullet and a dropped bullet (same height) land…
Convert 60 mph to m/s (1 mph = 0.447 m/s). One decimal.
Braking from 20 m/s to a stop at 5 m/s². Braking distance?
practice.hint: Use the equation with no time in it.

practice.q: Same truck, same braking (5 m/s²), but from 40 m/s. Braking distance?
practice.why: 1,600 ÷ 10 = **160 m**. Double the speed → **4×** the distance.

practice.q: A rock dropped off a bridge hits the water 3 s later. How high is the bridge? (g = 9.8, ignore air)
A ball is thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s. How many seconds until it reaches the top?
practice.why: v = v₀ + at → 0 = 19.6 − 9.8t → **t = 2 s**. (And another 2 s to come back down.)
practice.hint: At the top, v = 0. Up is positive, so a = −9.8.
